source.title: InstructRetro: Instruction Tuning post Retrieval-Augmented Pretraining
source.authors: Bo-Xin Wang; Wei Ping; Lawrence C. McAfee; Peng Xu; Bo Li; M. Shoeybi; Bryan Catanzaro

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out pretraining perplexity across model sizes and reports downstream accuracy across sizes, but it does not fit or test scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: The study's main results compare retrieval-augmented pretraining with GPT and report downstream benchmark scores; those comparisons do not by themselves test power-law form or compute-optimal allocation. The held-out perplexity size sweep (Figure 2) and the Natural Question size sweep (Figure 5) are included. Other downstream benchmark comparisons are not rows because they do not report a scaling relation.
record.test_reason: The study is a retrieval-augmentation paper, not a scaling-law study. It does include incidental model-size sweeps. Only the zero-shot Natural Question sweep (Fig. 5a, 2.25B–43B) gives a stated result on downstream scaling: the authors say performance of both GPT and Retro 'start to saturate'. The perplexity sweep (Fig. 2, 823M–43/48B) has no readable values and no fit, so it cannot test V1's power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Continuing GPT pretraining with retrieval on 100B tokens (Retro 48B) improves held-out perplexity over GPT at all sizes, with the gap not shrinking at 48B, for about 2.58% extra GPU hours. After instruction tuning, InstructRetro beats InstructGPT-RAG on short-form QA (+7%), long-form QA (+10%) and summarization (+16%). The decoder-only InstructRetro 43B performs comparably to the 48B model with its encoder.
record.recipe_differences: The study continues GPT pretraining with retrieval augmentation, then instruction-tunes models and evaluates perplexity and downstream tasks. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Natural Question size-sweep pattern depends on training stage: before instruction tuning, performance starts to saturate; after instruction tuning, the authors report a more pronounced retrieval benefit.

fits_no_version.finding: Retro-fitting has lower held-out perplexity than GPT and GPT-fitting at every size, matching GPT models about 4× larger. The gap does not shrink from 8B to 48B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retrieval-augmented continued pretraining gives a size-equivalent perplexity gain that persists with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction tuning removes the saturation seen in zero-shot NQ for pretrained models and enlarges Retro's advantage at 43/48B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent downstream saturation with scale can be an evaluation-format bottleneck that instruction tuning removes.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235 (2024)
record.problems: The relevant scaling results are shown in figures without numerical point values in the supplied text. The study does not fit scaling laws or report uncertainty for these sweeps; its downstream size-sweep evidence is limited to Natural Question.
record.rows_left_out: No separate downstream benchmark rows from Tables 1–3 were included because they compare retrieval-trained and GPT counterparts at selected sizes rather than report a scaling relation. The Figure 3 freezing/unfreezing ablation is also omitted because it compares training choices at fixed size, not the claim's scale relationships.

untested.parts: No power-law fit and no readable perplexity values. Size spans under two orders of magnitude, and tokens and compute are not varied.
No fixed-size shape comparison. The only related remark is that more Retro encoder layers did not improve perplexity, which is a preliminary result with no numbers.
No test of power-law form under retrieval pretraining or fine-tuning.
Only zero-shot Natural Question with pre-instruction-tuned models is swept over size. There is no fit to scale or loss, and no numbers are readable.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling evidence is incidental and figure-only. V1 rows stay cannot_determine, and there is no V1 verdict. The V6 verdict rests on the authors' wording about saturation, which they attribute to an instruction-following bottleneck rather than to scale itself.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies parameter count but does not fit a power law, test several orders of magnitude, or vary tokens and compute to test their loss relationships.
No losses fitted on small runs are used to predict larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Retrieval-augmented pretraining and instruction tuning are used, but the study does not test whether power-law forms hold across training regimes or modalities.
The downstream size sweep is on Natural Question; the study does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or allocation trends across counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot Natural Question EM, pretrained (not instruction-tuned) GPT and Retro, 2.25B–43/48B
relationships.reason: The authors state that zero-shot accuracy of both models 'start to saturate' as size grows. They attribute this to poor instruction following, i.e. it depends on evaluation format (F5-GPT-8B/22B/43B, F5-Retro-8B/22B/43B). The judgement rests on the text, not on plotted values.
relationships.display_finding: Zero-shot accuracy began saturating with size, which the authors attributed to poor instruction following in the evaluation format.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pre-instruction-tuning GPT and Retro size sweep on Natural Question
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that zero-shot performance starts to saturate with size and that retrieval's advantage also saturates; see F5-GPT-8B, F5-GPT-22B, F5-GPT-43B, F5-Retro-8B, F5-Retro-22B, and F5-Retro-43B.
